title: Kazakhstan's billion-dollar rare earths push faces familiar obstacles | The National
gist: Kazakhstan holds roughly 2 million tonnes of tungsten and a 20-million-tonne rare earth discovery, but landlocked geography, Soviet-era equipment, no oxide separation capacity and a weak grid mean it is not a realistic China substitute for the foreseeable future. The deeper constraint is capital: mining is low-margin, energy-intensive and takes up to 15 years, and US capital markets will not fund it absent a durable, policy-driven price environment - while a $1.6bn tungsten deal is already entangled in US political risk.

insights.claim: China controls about 60 percent of global rare earths output and up to 90 percent of refining capacity, giving it the ability to control critical minerals supply chains at will.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: The refining share, not the mining share, is the real chokepoint - value accrues to whoever builds separation and refining capacity outside China.
insights.quote: China has a tight grip on the critical minerals supply chain, wielding about 60 per cent of global rare earths output and up to 90 per cent of refining capacity.

insights.claim: China's expanded rare earth export restrictions from last year are currently shelved only until November, making that month a concrete catalyst date for supply-chain disruption.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: A dated expiry on a truce is tradeable: rare-earth-exposed names and downstream magnet users face a binary in November.
insights.quote: Those restrictions are currently shelved until November.

insights.claim: Public financing commitments for new critical minerals projects more than quadrupled to $65 billion between 2023 and 2025, according to IEA analysis cited in the piece.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: State capital, not private capital, is underwriting the diversification build-out - follow sovereign and DFI balance sheets to find where projects actually get built.
insights.quote: public financing commitments for new projects more than quadrupled to $65 billion between 2023 and 2025
insights.locator: The US and other countries are racing

insights.claim: Kazakhstan is a leading uranium producer, a top exporter of copper and zinc, and its government claims more than 9,500 mineral deposits including lithium and tantalum.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: Breadth of endowment makes Kazakhstan a perennial candidate for Western supply deals even when individual projects stall.
insights.quote: It is a leading uranium producer, a top exporter of copper and zinc, and its government claims to have more than 9,500 deposits of minerals including lithium, tantalum and other minerals.

insights.claim: Kazakhstan has proven resources or active production of about half the minerals the United States designates as critical for electrification and national security.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: Sets the theoretical ceiling of the Kazakh diversification story - about half the US critical list, not all of it.
insights.quote: It also has proven resources or active production of about half of the minerals listed by the US that are considered critical for electrification and national security.

insights.claim: Kazakh estimates put the country's tungsten resources at about two million tonnes, a metal used in Patriot and THAAD missiles drawn from a dwindling US munitions stockpile.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: Directly links Central Asian mining to the US missile replenishment cycle - tungsten supply is a defense-industrial input, not just an industrial metal.
insights.quote: about two million tonnes of tungsten, a dense metal used in Patriot and THAAD missiles that are part of a dwindling US munitions stockpile
insights.locator: This includes, according to Kazakh estimates

insights.claim: Last year's Zhana Kazakhstan discovery about 420km from Astana is estimated to contain more than 20 million tonnes of rare earth metals, but a resource estimate does not translate into production.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: Headline resource numbers move sentiment but not supply - the tradeable milestones are financing, processing and transport infrastructure.
insights.quote: The deposit is estimated to have more than 20 million tonnes of rare earth metals. But this does not necessarily translate into production.

insights.claim: The ultimate impact of the Zhana Kazakhstan discovery depends on how quickly the country can attract investment and develop processing and transport infrastructure, according to a Carnegie Russia Eurasia Centre fellow.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: Processing plus logistics - not geology - is the gating factor to watch for any Kazakh minerals investment thesis.
insights.quote: While the discovery may be strategically important, its ultimate impact will depend on how quickly Kazakhstan can attract investment and develop processing and transport infrastructure,

insights.claim: Kazakhstan is not a realistic substitute for China in the foreseeable future because it is landlocked, runs Soviet-era equipment and lacks advanced refining, according to Carnegie's Temur Umarov.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: Fade narratives that any single Central Asian country breaks China's rare earth grip this decade - diversification will be incremental and multi-country.
insights.quote: Kazakhstan is not a realistic substitute for China in the foreseeable future,

insights.claim: The Kazakh mining industry relies on outdated equipment and lacks processing and separation facilities for rare-earth oxides as well as environmentally friendly technology, and must also contend with a weak regional energy grid.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: Separation capacity and power supply are the two capex items that must be financed before any Kazakh REE tonnes reach Western buyers.
insights.quote: The country's mining industry continues to rely on outdated equipment and it lacks the processing and separation facilities for rare-earth oxides, as well as environmentally friendly technology. It also must contend with a weak regional energy grid.

insights.claim: Because it is landlocked, Kazakhstan depends on the Middle Corridor with more than 4,250km of rail lines, making exports costly and time-consuming, while the alternative route through Russia is a non-starter for Washington's security interests.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: Logistics cost is a permanent margin drag versus seaborne competitors - Middle Corridor rail capacity is the bottleneck asset to track.
insights.quote: The route contains more than 4,250km of rail lines, making it costly and time consuming to move exports.
insights.locator: Its geography adds another layer of difficulty

insights.claim: Even a sympathetic assessment concedes Kazakhstan is still far from being near a complete substitute for China, per a research fellow at the Arab Gulf States Institute.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: Consensus among independent analysts, bullish and bearish alike, is that substitution is partial - price relief from Kazakh supply should not be assumed.
insights.quote: It is still far from being near a complete substitute for China,

insights.claim: In June the US Export-Import Bank and the International Development Finance Corporation issued letters of interest totalling $1.6 billion to finance a deal between US-based Cove Capital and Kazakhstan's state mining company to develop the Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty tungsten deposits.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: US development finance is now underwriting foreign tungsten supply directly - a template for further state-backed offtake structures in critical minerals.
insights.quote: the US Export-Import Bank and International Development Finance Corporation wrote letters of interest adding up to $1.6 billion to finance a deal with US-based Cove Capital and Kazakhstan's state mining company to develop two tungsten deposits in Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty
insights.locator: In June, the US Export-Import Bank

insights.claim: Gulf states are moving into critical minerals as part of economic diversification, with Kazakhstan signing a mining cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia and Abu Dhabi's ADQ participating in the $1.8 billion Orion Consortium exploring Central Asian opportunities.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: Gulf sovereign capital is a competing bidder for the same Central Asian assets US agencies are financing - expect valuation support and geopolitical complexity.
insights.quote: Abu Dhabi's ADQ is also part of the $1.8 billion Orion Consortium exploring investment opportunities in Kazakhstan and across Central Asia.
insights.locator: Kazakhstan and Saudi Arabia signed an agreement

insights.claim: Rio Tinto and Barrick Gold are among the mining companies that have entered the Kazakh market, and investment in geological exploration has exceeded $1 billion since 2018 according to the country's industry minister.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: Major-miner presence validates the jurisdiction at the exploration stage; watch whether any converts exploration spend into committed processing capex.
insights.quote: mining companies Rio Tinto and Barrick Gold were among the firms to enter the Kazakh market
insights.locator: Speaking at the C5+1 Dialogue on Critical Minerals

insights.claim: Kazakhstan is embedding itself in US-backed diplomatic frameworks including the C5+1 summits, the Pax Silica initiative and the Abraham Accords, tying minerals access to a broader alignment bargain.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: Minerals deals are being bundled with diplomatic alignment - political shifts in either capital can reprice the commercial terms.
insights.quote: Kazakhstan has remained engaged in US-backed diplomatic efforts including the C5+1 summits, the Pax Silica initiative and the Abraham Accords.

insights.claim: Mining projects operate at low margins, require enormous upfront capital and can take up to 15 years to become operable, which magnifies every other Kazakh disadvantage.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: A 15-year lead time means today's policy urgency cannot produce supply inside the current political or commodity cycle.
insights.quote: Mining projects operate at low margins, require enormous amounts of capital up front and can take up to 15 years to become operable.

insights.claim: US capital markets have no significant appetite for low-margin, brute-force, energy-intensive mining activity absent a durable, policy-driven price environment, according to the Peterson Institute's Cullen Hendrix.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: The unlock for Western critical-minerals supply is a price floor or offtake guarantee, not more exploration headlines - watch for legislated price supports.
insights.quote: It is going to require investment in low margin, brute force, energy-intensive economic activities that US capital markets do not have a significant appetite for, absent a durable, policy-driven price environment,

insights.claim: Geopolitics cannot be removed from the critical minerals investment equation, meaning project economics must be underwritten with political risk as a first-order variable.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: Discount rates for mining in contested corridors should embed political risk explicitly rather than treating it as a tail scenario.
insights.quote: We obviously can't take geopolitics out of this equation,

insights.claim: The New York Times reported in late June that the families of President Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick could profit from the $1.6 billion tungsten deal, a claim the Trump Organisation denies.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: Conflict-of-interest exposure adds headline and reversal risk to a specific financing that other critical-minerals deals are being modelled on.
insights.quote: The New York Times reported in late June that the families of President Donald Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick could profit from the $1.6 billion tungsten deal.

insights.claim: Democratic politicians have opened investigations into the critical minerals deals, and those efforts could gain momentum if the party retakes either chamber of Congress in November's elections.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: November US midterms are a second dated catalyst for this sector, alongside the expiry of China's shelved export restrictions.
insights.quote: Those efforts could gain momentum if the party retakes either or both of the chambers of Congress in elections in November.

insights.claim: Production at the Kazakh tungsten mine is expected to begin in three and a half years, meaning Trump will be out of office before the asset is operational and a successor with different interests will decide whether to defend the investment.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: Political-cycle mismatch is the core underwriting risk: the sponsor administration will be gone before first production.
insights.quote: Regardless, Mr Trump will be out of office before the tungsten mine becomes operational. Production is expected to begin in three and a half years

insights.claim: There is no guarantee that US defence of private investments abroad continues into a new administration, a long-standing problem for Western companies that cannot count on Washington's backing when policy shifts, per Bloomberg Economics' Chris Kennedy.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: Sovereign-backing risk should be priced into any US-financed foreign mining project with a development timeline longer than one presidential term.
insights.quote: We've seen how different administrations approach questions of defending private US investments abroad

insights.claim: The Trump administration mobilises minerals investment by taking equity stakes across the value chain - Trilogy Metals in exploration and development, MP Materials in mining, ReElement Technologies in refining - rather than the grants and loans favoured under Biden.
insights.speaker: Kyle Fitzgerald
insights.so_what: Direct government equity changes the payoff profile for these specific names and signals which parts of the value chain Washington considers strategic.
insights.quote: the US government is taking equity stakes in companies across the value chain, from exploration and development with Trilogy Metals, to mining through MP Materials and refining through ReElement Technologies
insights.locator: The Trump administration's approach towards mobilising investment
